_readme: Lesson quizzes: 20 questions per lesson, pass mark 75%. Edit here, then run: python Tools/lesson-quizzes/build_lesson_quizzes.py. Types: mc (options + answer index), tf (answer true/false), match (pairs: [left, right]), order (items in the CORRECT order). {"ref": name} reuses an existing card from Assets/_Project/Data/QuizQuestions. Keep every id unique and never reuse an old id for a different question: Memorize progress is keyed by it.

questions.q: Which part is the main circuit board that every other part plugs into?
questions.why: The motherboard connects the CPU, memory, storage, graphics card and power, and carries data between them.

questions.q: Which part turns wall power into the steady DC voltages the components need?
questions.why: The PSU converts AC mains electricity into 12 V, 5 V and 3.3 V DC.

questions.q: Which part draws images, video and 3D graphics for the monitor?
questions.why: The GPU has thousands of small cores working in parallel, which is ideal for drawing frames.

questions.q: What is the job of the CPU cooler?
options: Pull heat away from the CPU
Supply power to the fans only
questions.why: Heat pipes carry heat from the CPU into metal fins, and a fan blows it away.

questions.q: What does the case do?
options: Holds and protects the parts and guides airflow
questions.why: The case has mounting points for every part, front-panel buttons and ports, and paths for air to flow through.

questions.q: RAM keeps its contents when the PC is switched off.
questions.why: RAM is temporary memory. It is cleared when the power goes off; files are kept on storage like an SSD.

questions.q: An SSD stores data in flash memory chips and has no moving parts.
questions.why: That is why SSDs are fast, quiet and tougher than spinning hard drives.

questions.q: Match each part to its job.
questions.why: Each part has one main job; together they make a working computer.

questions.q: Match each part to its job.
questions.why: The GPU draws, the motherboard connects, the cooler cools and the case holds it all.

questions.q: Where does the CPU fetch the instructions of a running program from?
questions.why: Programs are loaded from storage into RAM, and the CPU reads its instructions from there.

questions.q: Which upgrade makes games and files load faster from storage?
questions.why: Loading speed depends on how fast the storage can be read; an NVMe SSD is much faster than a hard drive.

questions.q: A powerful graphics card usually needs which extra connection?
questions.why: The PCIe slot alone can't supply enough power, so the card takes extra power straight from the PSU.

questions.q: Every component connects to the motherboard, either directly or through a cable.
questions.why: The motherboard is the hub: parts plug into its sockets, slots and headers.

questions.q: What does GPU stand for?
questions.why: The Graphics Processing Unit is the chip that draws images.

questions.q: What does PSU stand for?
questions.why: The Power Supply Unit provides power to every component.

questions.q: A CPU can run without a cooler if the PC is only on for a few minutes.
questions.why: A CPU can overheat within seconds without a cooler. Never power on without one fitted.

questions.q: Put the steps in order when you open a game.
order: Read from the SSD
Loaded into RAM
Processed by the CPU
Drawn by the GPU
Shown on the monitor
questions.why: Simplified, data flows from storage to memory, the CPU works on it, the GPU draws it, and the monitor shows it.

questions.q: What does CPU stand for?
questions.why: The Central Processing Unit runs the instructions of every program.

questions.q: Put the CPU's basic cycle in order.
order: Fetch an instruction
Decode it
Execute it
Store the result
questions.why: The CPU repeats fetch, decode, execute and store billions of times a second.

questions.q: How often does a CPU repeat its fetch-decode-execute cycle?
options: A few thousand times an hour
questions.why: A clock speed of a few gigahertz means billions of cycles every second.

questions.q: What does the small gold triangle on the corner of the CPU show?
options: Which way it goes into the socket
questions.why: Line up the CPU's triangle with the triangle on the socket and it drops in the right way round.

questions.q: Which socket does this app's CPU fit?
questions.why: The CPU and the motherboard in this app both use the AM5 socket.

questions.q: This CPU has 6 cores. What do several cores let it do?
options: Work on several tasks at the same time
questions.why: Each core can run its own work, so a multi-core CPU handles several tasks at once.

questions.q: A CPU needs a cooler and thermal paste to run safely.
questions.why: Without them the CPU overheats and slows down or shuts off.

questions.q: How should you hold a CPU?
options: By pressing on the lid with a screwdriver
questions.why: Touching the contacts can leave grease or bend them. Always hold the CPU by its edges.

questions.q: What do you do before lowering the CPU into the socket?
options: Put thermal paste in the socket
questions.why: The lever opens the socket. You close it again to lock the CPU in.

questions.q: This app's AM5 CPU works with DDR4 memory.
questions.why: AM5 CPUs work with DDR5 memory only.

questions.q: What is the metal lid on top of the CPU called?
questions.why: The heat spreader protects the chip and spreads its heat evenly into the cooler.

questions.q: What does the "65 W" in the CPU's specs tell you?
options: Roughly how much power it uses and heat it gives off
The size of its cooler fan
questions.why: The wattage helps you pick a cooler and a power supply that can keep up.

questions.q: What happens if a CPU gets too hot?
options: It slows itself down or shuts off to protect itself
It moves work to the cooler
questions.why: This is called thermal throttling. A good cooler prevents it.

questions.q: When lined up correctly, the CPU drops into the socket with no pressure.
questions.why: Lower it straight down and let it settle. Forcing it can bend the socket pins.

questions.q: The CPU doesn't sit flat in the socket. What should you do?
options: Lift it out and check the triangles line up
questions.why: A CPU that won't sit flat is almost always turned the wrong way.

questions.q: Match each CPU term to what it means.
pairs: Where the CPU sits on the board
Fills gaps between CPU and cooler
questions.why: These four terms come up every time you choose or install a CPU.

questions.q: In a gaming PC, which part does the CPU hand the drawing work to?
questions.why: The CPU prepares the game logic and the GPU draws the frames.

questions.q: A clock speed in gigahertz (GHz) tells you how many billions of cycles a core runs each second.
questions.why: 4 GHz means about four billion cycles per second, per core.

questions.q: What does RAM stand for?
questions.why: Random Access Memory holds the data the CPU is working on right now.

questions.q: When you switch off the PC, everything in RAM is cleared.
questions.why: RAM needs power to hold data. Save your work to storage before switching off.

questions.q: What does more RAM let you do?
options: Run more programs at once smoothly
Keep files when the PC is off
questions.why: More RAM means more room for running programs and open files.

questions.q: This app's RAM is rated 5600 MT/s. What does that describe?
questions.why: MT/s means mega-transfers per second: how fast data moves in and out of the stick.

questions.q: What does "16 GB" on a RAM stick describe?
options: How much data it can hold
questions.why: Gigabytes measure capacity: how much data the stick can hold at once.

questions.q: How should you hold a RAM stick?
questions.why: Touching the gold contacts can leave grease that causes a bad connection.

questions.q: Put the RAM install steps in order.
order: Open the clips at the ends of the slot
Line up the notch with the key in the slot
Press down firmly on both ends
Check both clips have clicked shut
questions.why: Open, line up, press, check: both clips closing tells you the stick is fully seated.

questions.q: A RAM stick can go into its slot either way round.
questions.why: The notch only lines up with the key in the slot one way.

questions.q: Why install RAM sticks in pairs?
options: So they run in dual-channel mode
Because one stick can't work alone
questions.why: In dual-channel mode the CPU talks to both sticks at once, which nearly doubles memory bandwidth.

questions.q: With two sticks on a four-slot board, which slots are usually recommended?
questions.why: Most boards run two sticks in dual-channel from A2 and B2. Check the manual to be sure.

questions.q: How is RAM different from storage like an SSD?
options: RAM is fast and temporary; storage keeps data with the power off
RAM keeps data with the power off; storage is temporary
RAM is slower than an SSD
questions.why: RAM is the short-term workspace; storage is the long-term filing cabinet.

questions.q: DDR5 RAM fits and works in a DDR4 motherboard.
questions.why: The notch sits in a different place and the electrical design differs, so the generations are not interchangeable.

questions.q: You press a stick in and only one clip closes. What does that mean?
options: It isn't fully seated; press firmly on both ends again
It belongs in a different slot
questions.why: A half-seated stick can stop the PC from starting. Both clips must click.

questions.q: Match each RAM label to what it means.
questions.why: These labels tell you if a stick fits your board and how much and how fast it is.

questions.q: A PC with too little RAM for its programs usually…
options: Slows down as it swaps data to storage
questions.why: When RAM is full, the system moves data to much slower storage, so everything feels sluggish.

questions.q: The notch on the bottom edge of a RAM stick stops it going in the wrong way.
questions.why: It also stops the wrong generation fitting the slot.

questions.q: Which part reads from and writes to RAM the most?
questions.why: The CPU constantly loads instructions and data from RAM and writes results back.

questions.q: How can you tell DDR4 from DDR5 by looking at a stick?
options: The sticker says DDR4 / PC4 or DDR5 / PC5
questions.why: The two look almost identical, so check the label. PC4 means DDR4 and PC5 means DDR5.

questions.q: What is the main job of the motherboard?
options: Connect all the parts and carry data between them
questions.why: Every part plugs into the motherboard, and its circuits carry power and data between them.

questions.q: What are the metal posts that hold the motherboard off the case called?
questions.why: Standoffs keep the back of the board from touching the metal case.

questions.q: Which CPU socket does this app's motherboard have?
questions.why: The board's AM5 socket matches the app's AM5 CPU.

questions.q: How many RAM (DIMM) slots does this motherboard have?
questions.why: It has four DDR5 DIMM slots.

questions.q: Where does an NVMe SSD plug in?
questions.why: An M.2 NVMe SSD plugs straight into the board with no cables.

questions.q: What does "ATX" in the motherboard's specs describe?
questions.why: ATX is a standard board size. The case must support it.

questions.q: The motherboard's rear ports poke out through the I/O shield at the back of the case.
questions.why: The I/O shield fills the gap around the ports and keeps dust out.

questions.q: Put the motherboard install steps in order.
order: Install the I/O shield (if separate)
Check the standoffs match the screw holes
Lower the board in at an angle
Screw it down, snug but not tight
questions.why: Shield first, then standoffs, then the board, then the screws.

questions.q: How tight should the motherboard screws be?
options: Loose so the board can move
questions.why: Overtightening can crack the board; loose screws let it move. Snug is right.

questions.q: What is the 8-pin connector near the CPU socket for?
questions.why: The EPS 8-pin feeds the CPU. It sits near the socket, usually at the top-left of the board.

questions.q: What plugs into the CPU_FAN header?
questions.why: The board controls the cooler fan's speed from this header and warns if it isn't spinning.

questions.q: You can screw the motherboard straight onto the bare case wall with no standoffs.
questions.why: Without standoffs the circuits on the back would touch the metal case and short.

questions.q: Which slot does the graphics card use?
questions.why: The long PCIe x16 slot gives the graphics card the most bandwidth.

questions.q: Match each header to what plugs into it.
questions.why: Headers are the small pin blocks the case's front-panel cables plug into.

questions.q: Why lower the motherboard in at an angle?
options: So the rear ports slide into the I/O shield first
So the screws fall into place
questions.why: Tilting it lets the ports line up with the shield before the board settles on the standoffs.

questions.q: The chipset is a chip on the motherboard that manages connections like USB and SATA.
questions.why: It works alongside the CPU to run the board's extra ports and slots.

questions.q: What keeps the BIOS clock and settings when the PC is unplugged?
options: A coin-cell battery on the motherboard
questions.why: The small CMOS battery powers the clock and settings while the PC has no power.

questions.q: What does an SSD store data in?
questions.why: Flash memory keeps data without power and has no moving parts.

questions.q: How does a hard drive (HDD) store data?
questions.why: A hard drive has spinning disks and a moving arm, which makes it slower than an SSD.

questions.q: Why is an SSD much faster than a hard drive?
options: Data is read electronically, with no moving parts
questions.why: A hard drive must wait for its disk and arm to move; an SSD doesn't.

questions.q: "M.2 2280" tells you the SSD is…
questions.why: The number is the size: 22 mm wide and 80 mm long, the most common M.2 length.

questions.q: At about what angle do you insert an M.2 SSD into its slot?
questions.why: Insert it at about 30 degrees, press it flat, then fix it with the screw or latch.

questions.q: Overtightening the tiny M.2 screw can damage the drive or the board.
questions.why: The screw only needs to hold the drive down. Turn it until it stops, then stop.

questions.q: What does an NVMe SSD use to talk to the CPU?
questions.why: PCIe is the same fast connection the graphics card uses, which is why NVMe drives are so quick.

questions.q: About how fast can a SATA SSD read data at best?
questions.why: SATA tops out around 550 MB/s. NVMe drives can be ten times faster.

questions.q: Where is the operating system usually installed in a new build?
questions.why: The OS on a fast NVMe SSD makes start-up and app loading quick.

questions.q: Unlike RAM, storage keeps your files when the PC is turned off.
questions.why: Storage is non-volatile: it holds data without power.

questions.q: Where can a 2.5-inch SATA SSD be mounted?
options: In a drive bay, a bracket or the PSU basement
questions.why: It's a small boxed drive that sits in a mounting spot and connects with cables.

questions.q: Match each drive to how it connects or works.
pairs: Needs SATA power and data cables
questions.why: All three keep files without power, but they differ a lot in speed and fitting.

questions.q: Which is the cheapest way to store lots of photos and backups?
questions.why: Hard drives are slower but cost far less per gigabyte, which suits big archives.

questions.q: Hold drives by their edges and don't drop them.
questions.why: A drop can damage a drive, especially a hard drive with moving parts.

questions.q: Which key does the M.2 slot for NVMe SSDs use?
questions.why: NVMe SSDs use the M-key slot; A and E keys are for things like Wi-Fi cards.

questions.q: Which slot does a graphics card use?
questions.why: The long PCIe x16 slot gives the card the bandwidth it needs.

questions.q: Why are graphics cards so good at drawing game frames?
options: Thousands of small cores work in parallel
They have one very fast core
They have a large hard drive
questions.why: A frame has millions of pixels, and many small cores can work on them at the same time.

questions.q: Which extra power cable does this app's graphics card need?
questions.why: The card takes extra power from an 8-pin PCIe cable on top of what the slot provides.

questions.q: The EPS 8-pin CPU cable and the 8-pin PCIe graphics cable are interchangeable.
questions.why: They look alike but are wired differently. Use the cable labeled for each part.

questions.q: Put the graphics card install steps in order.
order: Remove the expansion slot covers
Open the PCIe slot latch
Press the card down until the latch clicks
Screw the bracket in and connect PCIe power
questions.why: Make room, open the latch, seat the card, then secure and power it.

questions.q: Which PCIe x16 slot should the graphics card usually go in?
options: The top one, nearest the CPU
questions.why: The top x16 slot is normally wired with the most lanes straight to the CPU.

questions.q: Why support a long, heavy graphics card?
options: So it doesn't sag and stress the slot
questions.why: Over time a heavy card can bend and damage the slot. A support bracket prevents that.

questions.q: What is the graphics card's own memory called?
questions.why: VRAM holds the textures and frames the GPU is working on.

questions.q: Where does the graphics card send its finished frames?
options: To the monitor, through its display ports
questions.why: The monitor cable plugs into the ports on the card's bracket.

questions.q: In a gaming PC, the graphics card usually uses more power than any other part.
questions.why: That's why the card's power needs decide what size PSU you buy.

questions.q: Where do the graphics card's display ports come out of the case?
options: Through the expansion slot opening at the back
Through the top of the case
questions.why: The card's bracket replaces the slot covers you removed at the back of the case.

questions.q: The monitor is plugged into the motherboard's HDMI and shows nothing. The PC has a graphics card. Most likely fix?
options: Plug the monitor into the graphics card instead
questions.why: With a graphics card fitted, the motherboard's video ports are usually switched off.

questions.q: In a standard tower case, the graphics card's fans face down toward the bottom of the case.
questions.why: They pull in cooler air from below and push it through the card's heatsink.

questions.q: Match each part of the graphics card to its job.
pairs: Screws to the case and holds the ports
Takes extra power from the PSU
questions.why: Knowing these parts helps you install the card and find its connections.

questions.q: What does the latch at the end of the PCIe slot do?
options: Clicks to lock the card in place
questions.why: Listen for the click; it tells you the card is fully seated.

questions.q: How do you remove a graphics card?
options: Unscrew the bracket, press the slot latch, then lift
Pull hard until it comes out
questions.why: The latch holds the card in. Press it while lifting gently so nothing breaks.

questions.q: Integrated graphics means video is handled by the CPU instead of a separate card.
questions.why: Many CPUs have basic graphics built in, but a separate card is much faster for games.

questions.q: The "650 W PSU" chip on this graphics card means…
options: The whole PC needs at least a 650 W power supply
questions.why: It's the maker's recommended PSU size for a whole system with this card.

questions.q: What does a power supply do?
options: Converts AC wall power into DC for the parts
questions.why: Components need steady low-voltage DC, not the AC that comes from the wall.

questions.q: Which DC voltages does a PSU supply?
questions.why: 12 V powers the CPU and GPU; 5 V and 3.3 V power smaller parts.

questions.q: Where should the PSU's switch be while you build?
questions.why: Keep it off and unplugged until every part is installed.

questions.q: In a case with a bottom vent, which way should the PSU fan face?
questions.why: Facing the vent lets the PSU breathe cool air from outside the case.

questions.q: Put the PSU install steps in order.
order: Set the switch to O and unplug it
Slide it into the bottom bay, fan facing down
Screw it in from the back of the case
Route the cables through the grommets
questions.why: Make it safe, place it, fix it, then route the cables.

questions.q: An 80+ Gold PSU is efficient and wastes less power as heat.
questions.why: The 80+ ratings (Bronze, Gold, Platinum and so on) measure efficiency.

questions.q: This app's PSU is rated 700 W. What does that mean?
options: It can supply up to about 700 W to the parts
questions.why: The rating is the most it can deliver. The PC only draws what it needs at the time.

questions.q: What is a modular PSU?
options: One whose cables plug in and out as needed
One you can open and repair
One that works without wall power
questions.why: Only plugging in the cables you need keeps the build tidy.

questions.q: How do PSU cables reach the parts neatly?
options: Over the top of the graphics card
questions.why: Grommets let cables pass behind the motherboard tray, which keeps airflow clear.

questions.q: A power supply turns DC into AC.
questions.why: It's the other way round: AC from the wall becomes DC for the parts.

questions.q: Which PSU cable powers a SATA SSD?
questions.why: The wide SATA power connector feeds 2.5-inch drives.

questions.q: Where does the 24-pin cable from the PSU go?
questions.why: It supplies the motherboard's main power.

questions.q: Why buy a PSU from a trusted brand?
options: A poor PSU can fail and damage other parts
questions.why: Every part depends on the PSU, so a cheap unit is a risk to the whole PC.

questions.q: On the PSU switch, I means on and O means off.
questions.why: These are the standard power symbols.

questions.q: Where is the PSU usually mounted in a modern case?
options: At the bottom, under the PSU shroud
On top of the graphics card
questions.why: A bottom mount keeps the heavy PSU low and hides its cables.

questions.q: Match each PSU marking to what it means.
questions.why: These markings tell you how to switch it and what it can deliver.

questions.q: A PSU smells burnt or crackles. What should you do?
options: Switch off, unplug it and replace it, never open it
questions.why: Capacitors inside can hold a dangerous charge. A faulty PSU should be replaced, not repaired.

questions.q: A CPU only works in a motherboard whose socket…
options: Is the same color as the CPU
questions.why: An AM5 CPU needs an AM5 board, an LGA1700 CPU needs an LGA1700 board, and so on.

questions.q: Which CPU fits an AM5 motherboard?
questions.why: The socket name must match exactly, even between generations from the same maker.

questions.q: An AM4 CPU fits an AM5 socket because both are AMD.
questions.why: AM4 and AM5 are different sockets with different pin layouts.

questions.q: Which memory does an AM5 motherboard use?
questions.why: AM5 boards and CPUs support DDR5 only.

questions.q: What physically stops a DDR4 stick going into a DDR5 slot?
options: The notch is in a different place
questions.why: The notch position differs between generations, so the wrong one won't seat.

questions.q: The compatibility checker shows green when two parts work together.
questions.why: Green means their specs match.

questions.q: What does yellow mean in the compatibility checker?
options: Check required: it may work, but look closer
questions.why: Yellow flags something worth double-checking before you buy or build.

questions.q: What does red mean in the compatibility checker?
options: Incompatible: these parts won't work together
questions.why: Red means a spec doesn't match, like the wrong socket or memory type.

questions.q: You pair this app's AM5 CPU with the DDR4 stick. What does the checker show?
questions.why: AM5 needs DDR5, so DDR4 can't work with it.

questions.q: What must a CPU cooler have to fit your motherboard?
options: A mounting bracket for its socket
questions.why: Coolers attach around the socket, so the bracket must match it, like AM5 here.

questions.q: Where do you check which CPUs a motherboard supports?
options: The motherboard maker's CPU support list
questions.why: Makers publish CPU support lists, including any BIOS version needed.

questions.q: The motherboard's form factor, like ATX, must be supported by the case.
questions.why: The case's standoffs and rear opening are laid out for certain board sizes.

questions.q: An ATX motherboard needs a case that supports…
questions.why: A case built only for smaller boards won't have the space or screw holes.

questions.q: Intel sockets have names like "LGA1700". What does LGA mean?
options: Land Grid Array: pins in the socket, flat pads on the CPU
questions.why: With LGA, the delicate pins are in the socket, so handle the board's socket with care.

questions.q: On AM5, the pins are in the socket and the CPU has flat contact pads.
questions.why: AM5 is an LGA socket, so don't touch the socket pins or drop anything into it.

questions.q: Match each pair of parts to what must match between them.
questions.why: These four checks catch most compatibility mistakes.

questions.q: When might you need a BIOS update before building?
options: When a newer CPU goes on an older board with the same socket
questions.why: An older BIOS may not recognize a CPU that came out after the board.

questions.q: You fit RAM rated faster than the board supports. What happens?
options: It runs at a speed the board supports
questions.why: Memory runs at the fastest speed both the stick and the board support.

questions.q: You can mix DDR4 and DDR5 sticks in the same motherboard.
questions.why: A board supports one generation only, and the notches won't let the other fit.

questions.q: What is the best first step before buying parts?
options: Check the CPU, motherboard and RAM are compatible
Buy the biggest PSU you can find
questions.why: These three must match each other; everything else is chosen around them.

questions.q: What is a power budget?
options: Adding up the parts' power needs to choose a big enough PSU
The money you spend on the PSU
questions.why: Totaling what the parts need tells you how much wattage the PSU must supply.

questions.q: Which parts use the most power in a gaming PC?
options: The graphics card and the CPU
questions.why: These two do the heavy work, so they dominate the power budget.

questions.q: The graphics card needs a 650 W PSU and you have 700 W. Result?
options: Too much power will damage it
questions.why: 700 W covers the 650 W recommendation with a little headroom.

questions.q: The graphics card needs at least 650 W and your PSU is exactly 650 W. Is that a good choice?
options: It meets the minimum, but a bit more is safer
questions.why: Meeting the minimum works, but a little headroom covers power spikes and future upgrades.

questions.q: A PSU below the graphics card maker's recommendation is fine, as long as the PC turns on.
questions.why: It may start, then crash or shut down when the GPU works hard.

questions.q: Why leave headroom (extra wattage) on a PSU?
options: For power spikes and upgrades, and it runs cooler and quieter
questions.why: A PSU working below its limit is more efficient, cooler and longer lasting.

questions.q: A common rule of thumb for PSU headroom is…
questions.why: That margin covers spikes and small upgrades without paying for a PSU you'll never use.

questions.q: This app's CPU is rated 65 W. What is that number useful for?
options: Estimating how much power the CPU needs
Knowing how much RAM it supports
questions.why: You add the CPU's wattage to the rest of the parts in your power budget.

questions.q: What can happen if the PSU is too weak?
options: The PC crashes, restarts or shuts down under load
questions.why: When the parts ask for more than the PSU can give, it protects itself by cutting out.

questions.q: The W in 700 W stands for watts, a unit of power.
questions.why: Watts measure how much power is supplied or used.

questions.q: Compared with 80+ Bronze, an 80+ Gold PSU…
questions.why: Gold units turn more of the wall power into useful DC power.

questions.q: CPU 65 W + graphics card 220 W + other parts 75 W. What is the total?
With a 360 W total, which PSU is the most sensible choice?
questions.why: 450 W gives about 25% headroom. 300 W is too small, 360 W leaves none, and 1,600 W is wasted money.

questions.q: A PSU far bigger than you need, like 1,600 W for a 300 W PC, wastes money.
questions.why: You pay for capacity you'll never use, and very lightly loaded PSUs are less efficient.

questions.q: Which part of this app warns you when the PSU is too weak for the graphics card?
questions.why: The Compatibility tab compares the PSU's wattage with what the graphics card needs.

questions.q: A power-hungry graphics card needs the PSU to have enough…
questions.why: Big cards can need two or three PCIe power connectors, so check the PSU has them.

questions.q: Match each power-budget term to its meaning.
pairs: How hard the PC is working
questions.why: These terms are all you need to read a PSU spec sheet.

questions.q: A PC uses its full power budget all the time, even when idle.
questions.why: Power use rises and falls with load. Idle use is far below the maximum.

questions.q: Your new graphics card needs a 750 W PSU but you have 700 W. What should you do?
questions.why: Follow the card maker's recommendation, or the PC may be unstable under load.

questions.q: Where do you find a graphics card's recommended PSU wattage?
options: On the maker's website or the box
questions.why: The card's specifications list its recommended system power.

questions.q: Why is static electricity a danger to PC parts?
options: A tiny spark can damage chips without you noticing
questions.why: Your body can carry a charge strong enough to harm chips even if you never feel it.

questions.q: What does an anti-static wrist strap do?
options: Keeps you at the same charge as the case, so no spark jumps
questions.why: Clipped to bare metal on the case, it stops static building up between you and the parts.

questions.q: What is the best surface to build on?
questions.why: Hard surfaces don't build static, and small screws don't get lost.

questions.q: Unplug the PC from the wall before working inside it.
questions.why: Never work on a PC that is connected to mains power.

questions.q: Which tool will you use most when building a PC?
questions.why: Most PC screws are Phillips #2: case, motherboard, PSU and graphics card.

questions.q: Why use a small bowl or magnetic tray?
options: To keep small screws from getting lost
questions.why: PC screws are tiny and easy to lose. Keep each set together.

questions.q: Why does good lighting matter?
options: Small labels, pins and screws are easier to see
questions.why: Many mistakes come from misreading a tiny label or missing a bent pin.

questions.q: Keep drinks well away from your build area.
questions.why: One spill can ruin parts.

questions.q: Where should parts stay until you install them?
options: In their anti-static bags and boxes
Stacked on top of each other
questions.why: The bags protect against static and the boxes against knocks.

questions.q: How should you pick up a component?
options: By its edges, avoiding contacts and chips
questions.why: Edges are safe to touch; contacts and chips are sensitive to grease and static.

questions.q: Wool and synthetic clothing can build up static.
questions.why: Cotton is a better choice for building.

questions.q: What should you take off the case before you start?
options: Both side panels, with the screws stored safely
questions.why: Open sides give you room to work and light to see.

questions.q: What is a good idea before you start building?
options: Lay out and check all the parts and manuals
Switch the PC on to test it
Put thermal paste on every part
questions.why: Checking everything first means no surprises halfway through.

questions.q: Put these workspace steps in order.
order: Clear a hard, well-lit table
Lay the case on its side
Remove both side panels and store the screws
Touch bare metal on the case before handling parts
questions.why: Prepare the space, then the case, then discharge yourself right before touching parts.

questions.q: You drop a screw inside the case. What should you do?
options: Find and remove it before powering on
Shake the case while it's on
Power on to see if it matters
questions.why: A loose screw can short the motherboard when the power comes on.

questions.q: A cluttered table makes it more likely you'll lose screws or knock parts off.
questions.why: A clear space keeps parts safe and easy to find.

questions.q: Match each item to why you use it.
questions.why: A small kit like this is all most builds need.

questions.q: Why keep pets away from the build area?
options: Fur, dust and static get into parts, and pets knock things over
questions.why: Fur carries static and dust, and curious pets can send parts flying.

questions.q: How much thermal paste is usually enough?
options: A pea-sized dot in the middle
Enough to cover the whole board
questions.why: The cooler's pressure spreads a small dot into a thin, even layer.

questions.q: Why use thermal paste?
options: It fills tiny gaps so heat flows from CPU to cooler
questions.why: Air in the gaps would block heat. Paste conducts it much better.

questions.q: Many coolers come with thermal paste already on the base.
questions.why: Check before adding more. If it's pre-applied, you don't need extra.

questions.q: What must you remove from a new cooler's base before fitting it?
questions.why: Leaving the film on blocks heat, and the CPU will overheat.

questions.q: Which header does the cooler's fan cable plug into?
questions.why: The board watches CPU_FAN and warns or stops if the cooler fan isn't spinning.

questions.q: Which goes in first: the CPU or the cooler?
questions.why: The cooler sits on top of the CPU, so the CPU must be in and locked first.

questions.q: Put the core install steps in order.
order: Seat the CPU and close the lever
Fit the cooler's mounting bracket
Check thermal paste is on the CPU
Place the cooler and tighten screws diagonally
Connect the fan to CPU_FAN
questions.why: CPU, bracket, paste, cooler, fan cable.

questions.q: Why tighten cooler screws a little at a time, diagonally?
options: For even pressure, so the cooler sits flat
So it's easier to remove later
To spread the paste on the RAM
questions.why: Uneven pressure leaves a gap on one side, and the CPU runs hot.

questions.q: What should you check about RAM when fitting a large air cooler?
options: The cooler doesn't block or touch the RAM slots
The RAM color matches the cooler
The RAM weighs less than the cooler
questions.why: Big tower coolers can overhang the slots nearest the CPU, so check the clearance.

questions.q: You should put thermal paste on the RAM sticks too.
questions.why: Paste only goes between the CPU and its cooler.

questions.q: How do you know a RAM stick is fully seated?
questions.why: If a clip is still open, press firmly on that end until it clicks.

questions.q: What do the cooler's heat pipes do?
options: Carry heat from the CPU into the fins
questions.why: They move heat up into the fin stack, where the fan blows it away.

questions.q: Which way should a tower cooler's fan usually blow?
questions.why: Front-to-back airflow carries the CPU's heat straight out of the case.

questions.q: You can reuse the old thermal paste after taking the cooler off.
questions.why: Clean off the old paste and apply fresh paste before refitting.

questions.q: What do you clean old thermal paste off with?
options: Isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free cloth
questions.why: Isopropyl alcohol dissolves paste and dries quickly without leaving residue.

questions.q: What state should the CPU socket lever be in before fitting the cooler?
questions.why: The lever holds the CPU in place; the cooler goes on only after it's locked.

questions.q: Match each step to the part it involves.
questions.why: These four actions are the heart of the core install.

questions.q: It's normal for RAM to need firm pressure before the clips click.
questions.why: Press evenly on both ends. It takes more force than most people expect.

questions.q: Why does the 24-pin cable only fit one way?
options: Its pins are keyed and it has a latch
It is shorter on one side
questions.why: Shaped pins and the latch make wrong-way insertion impossible.

questions.q: How do you know the 24-pin cable is locked in?
options: The latch clicks over the tab
questions.why: Listen for the click, then tug gently to check.

questions.q: Put the 24-pin connection steps in order.
order: Route the cable through the grommet beside the header
Line up the latch with the tab on the header
Push straight in until it clicks
Tug gently to check it's locked
questions.why: Route, line up, push, check.

questions.q: Where is the EPS 8-pin CPU power connector on most motherboards?
questions.why: It's close to the socket to feed the CPU. Route its cable before fitting a big cooler.

questions.q: Where do the case's power switch, reset and LED wires plug in?
questions.why: These small connectors share the front-panel header, usually at the bottom-right of the board.

questions.q: Front-panel LED connectors have a + and a − side, so direction matters.
questions.why: Plugged in backwards, the light simply stays off. Check the + marking.

questions.q: The power switch connector works either way round.
questions.why: A switch just closes a circuit, so it has no + or − side.

questions.q: Where do you check which front-panel pins go where?
options: The motherboard manual or the labels printed on the board
questions.why: Layouts differ between boards, so always check the diagram.

questions.q: Where does the case's front USB 3.0 cable plug in?
questions.why: It's a wide, keyed header. Line it up carefully, as its pins bend easily.

questions.q: What does the HD_AUDIO header connect?
options: The case's front headphone and mic jacks
questions.why: It brings the board's audio to the front of the case.

questions.q: Why route cables behind the motherboard tray?
options: A tidier build and better airflow
It's needed for power to work
questions.why: Hidden cables don't block fans or trap heat.

questions.q: Match each front-panel connector to what it controls.
questions.why: The labels on the small connectors tell you which button or light they belong to.

questions.q: A case fan can plug into a SYS_FAN (or CHA_FAN) header.
questions.why: System and chassis fan headers power and control the case fans.

questions.q: Pressing the case power button does nothing. A likely cause?
options: The power switch connector is on the wrong pins
questions.why: If POWER SW isn't on the right two pins, the button can't start the PC.

questions.q: What are the rubber grommets in the case for?
questions.why: They line the cable holes so sharp metal edges can't cut the cables.

questions.q: Which cable connects a SATA SSD to the motherboard for data?
questions.why: The narrow SATA data cable goes from the drive to a SATA port on the board.

questions.q: Pull cable ties as tight as possible, even if they pinch the cables.
questions.why: Tie cables snugly but don't crush them. Pinched cables can be damaged.

questions.q: Why check every connection before the first power-on?
options: A loose or missing cable is the commonest reason a new build won't start
questions.why: A two-minute check saves a lot of troubleshooting.

questions.q: What should you do right before the first power-on?
options: Check every cable and that nothing is loose inside
Put paste on the graphics card
questions.why: A final look catches unplugged cables and stray screws.

questions.q: Put the first-boot steps in order.
order: Connect the monitor, keyboard and mouse
Plug in the power cable
Switch the PSU to I (on)
Press the case's power button
questions.why: Connect everything, then power, then the switch, then the button.

questions.q: What is POST?
options: The Power-On Self-Test that checks the hardware at start-up
questions.why: During POST the motherboard checks the CPU, memory and graphics before loading anything.

questions.q: What is the BIOS (UEFI)?
options: Firmware on the motherboard that starts the PC and holds its settings
questions.why: It runs before the operating system and lets you check and change hardware settings.

questions.q: Which key usually opens the BIOS during start-up?
questions.why: Press it repeatedly as soon as the PC powers on. The start screen usually says which key.

questions.q: If the fans spin, everything is working perfectly.
questions.why: Fans only show there is power. The PC can still fail POST with no picture.

questions.q: The PC turns on but the monitor stays black. What should you check first?
options: The monitor cable is in the graphics card and the right input is selected
questions.why: The cable in the wrong port, or the monitor on the wrong input, is the most common cause.

questions.q: Fans spin, there's no picture, and the DRAM debug light is on. What should you try?
options: Reseat the RAM so both clips click
questions.why: The DRAM light points to memory. A stick that isn't fully seated is the usual culprit.

questions.q: Nothing happens at all when you press the power button. What should you check?
options: The PSU switch, the power cable and the POWER SW connector
questions.why: No reaction at all usually means no power is reaching the board, or the button isn't connected.

questions.q: Debug lights on the motherboard (CPU, DRAM, VGA, BOOT) show which part stopped the start-up.
questions.why: The light that stays on tells you where to look first.

questions.q: What should you check in the BIOS on the first boot?
options: That it sees the CPU, all the RAM and your drives
questions.why: If something is missing from the list, it isn't connected or seated properly.

questions.q: What is the XMP or EXPO setting in the BIOS for?
options: Running the RAM at its rated speed
questions.why: Without it, RAM often runs at a slower default speed.

questions.q: The BIOS shows the CPU above 90 °C while idle. What is the likely cause?
options: The cooler isn't seated, its fan is unplugged, or the film was left on
questions.why: An idle CPU should be far cooler. Recheck the cooler before using the PC.

questions.q: After checking the BIOS, you install an operating system such as Windows or Linux on the SSD.
questions.why: A new PC needs an operating system before you can use it.

questions.q: How do you usually install an operating system on a new PC?
options: From a USB flash drive with the installer on it
questions.why: You prepare the installer on a USB stick on another computer, then start the new PC from it.

questions.q: Match each debug light to what it points to.
questions.why: Each light narrows down where the start-up stopped.

questions.q: The PC restarts on its own while gaming. What is a possible cause?
options: The PSU is too weak or the CPU is overheating
questions.why: Heavy load exposes weak power and poor cooling.

questions.q: If something smells burnt at first boot, switch off at the wall immediately.
questions.why: Cut the power first, then look for the cause with the PC unplugged.
